{{Short description|American mathematician and economist}}
'''Mildred Ginsberg Goldberger''' (23 March 1923 – 11 September 2006) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[economist]].

== Early life and education ==
Mildred Ginsberg was born in [[Wichita Falls, Texas]], on March 23, 1923.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Mildred (Ginsberg) Goldberger - Nuclear Museum |url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/mildred-ginsberg-goldberger/ |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=ahf.nuclearmuseum.org |language=en-US}}</ref> She received her B.A. in mathematics from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign]], in 1943. After graduation, she continued her education, taking graduate courses in math, physics, and economics at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2007 |title=MILDRED G. GOLDBERGER {{!}} 1934 – 2006 |url=https://calteches.library.caltech.edu/700/2/Obituaries.pdf |journal=Engineering & Science |volume=2}}</ref>

== Career ==
During WWII, Goldberger served as a research assistant and computer for the theoretical physics division of the [[Manhattan Project]] at the Metallurgical Laboratory at the University of Chicago.<ref name=":0" /> She was one of ten women to sign the [[Szilard Petition]] against the use of a nuclear bomb on Japan.<ref name=":0" />

After WWII, Goldberger held a variety of posts, including chief of the computation group for the University of Chicago Air Force Project, course manager for the [[Princeton University]] Math Department, economics instructor at [[Rutgers University]], research analyst with the New Jersey Department of Higher Education, and research associate with the [[Princeton University|Princeton]] Center for Environmental and Energy Studies.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Shirlee Smith {{!}} Women's History- Mildred Goldberger Set An Example – Pasadena Now |url=https://pasadenanow.com/main/shirlee-smith-womens-history-mildred-goldberger-set-an-example |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=pasadenanow.com}}</ref>

Goldberger served as the editor for "Scientific View," the [[Los Angeles Times]]' science column, and ensured that contributions from women scientists and science writers were published regularly.<ref name=":1" />

Goldberger became First Lady of [[CalTech]] when her husband, [[Marvin Leonard Goldberger|Marvin "Murph" Goldberger]], was appointed president in 1978. They stayed at the university until 1987. While there, she started a program with the CalTech Women's Club to act as "grandmothers" to foster children in the welfare system in their community.<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
Mildred Ginsberg married physicist Marvin Goldberger, whom she met while working on the Manhattan Project.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marvin L. Goldberger Papers, 1945 - 2012 - OAC |url=https://oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/c80p1570/ |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=oac.cdlib.org |language=en}}</ref> She died in [[La Jolla, California]], on September 11, 2006.<ref name=":0" />
